motor-starting-current-calculator.name: Motor Starting Current Calculator
motor-starting-current-calculator.tagline: Estimate a motor's full-load current and inrush starting current from its rating plate.
motor-starting-current-calculator.metaDescription: Free motor starting current calculator: estimate full-load current and inrush current for single and three-phase motors. Size breakers and cables safely.
motor-starting-current-calculator.keywords: motor starting current calculator, inrush current calculator, motor full load current, NEMA locked rotor current
motor-starting-current-calculator.quickAnswer: An induction motor draws roughly 5 to 7 times its full-load current at start-up. Full-load current = Power (W) / (root-3 x Voltage x efficiency x power factor) for three-phase motors. Example: a 10 HP, 415 V three-phase motor at 88% efficiency and 0.85 power factor draws about 13.87 A at full load and about 83.2 A at start with a 6x multiplier. Size breakers, contactors, and cables for the inrush value, not the running current.
keyFacts: Direct-on-line starting current is typically 5 to 7 times the full-load current for standard induction motors.
Full-load current depends on real power output, voltage, efficiency, and power factor - not just horsepower.
Three-phase current divides by root 3 (1.732); single-phase motors draw root-3 times more for the same power.
NEMA code letters on the nameplate define locked-rotor kVA per HP, which pins down the exact starting current.
Soft starters and star-delta starters reduce inrush to about 2 to 4 times full-load current.
Undersized protection trips on start-up; oversized protection may not protect the motor at all.
howTo: Enter the motor's rated power from the nameplate, in HP or kW.
Select single-phase or three-phase, then enter the supply voltage.
Enter the nameplate efficiency and power factor (defaults 88% and 0.85 suit most standard motors).
Set the starting-current multiplier: 6 is typical for direct-on-line starting, 2 to 4 for star-delta or soft start.
Use the inrush result to select breaker, contactor, overload relay, and cable sizes.
motor-starting-current-calculator.formula:
Three-phase: I = P / (1.732 x V x efficiency x power factor), with P in watts.
Single-phase: I = P / (V x efficiency x power factor).
Starting current = Full-load current x starting multiplier.
Example: 10 HP = 7,460 W; 7,460 / (1.732 x 415 x 0.88 x 0.85) = 13.87 A; 13.87 x 6 = 83.2 A inrush.
motor-starting-current-calculator.workedExample:
10 HP motor, 415 V, three-phase, 88% efficiency, 0.85 power factor, multiplier 6:
1. Convert power: 10 x 746 = 7,460 W.
2. Full-load current: 7,460 / (1.732 x 415 x 0.88 x 0.85) = 7,460 / 537.66 = 13.87 A.
3. Starting current: 13.87 x 6 = 83.2 A.
4. Starting kVA (3-phase): 1.732 x 415 x 83.2 / 1,000 = 59.8 kVA.
So the breaker and contactor must handle an 83 A inrush even though the motor runs at 14 A.
benefits: Sizes protection correctly the first time, avoiding nuisance tripping on start-up.
Covers single-phase and three-phase motors with one tool.
Works from standard nameplate data, no clamp meter needed for planning.
Adjustable multiplier handles direct-on-line, star-delta, and soft starters.
limitations: Estimates only. Real inrush depends on rotor design, load inertia, and supply impedance.
Uses nameplate efficiency and power factor, which vary with actual loading.
Not a substitute for an electrician's verification before finalizing protection and cable sizes.
Does not model variable-frequency drives, which control starting current electronically.

faqs.q: Why does a motor draw so much current at start?
faqs.a: At standstill the rotor is not turning, so there is no back-EMF to oppose the supply voltage. The motor looks almost like a short circuit until it spins up and back-EMF builds, which is why current spikes to 5 to 7 times the running value for a fraction of a second to a few seconds.

Use 6 for direct-on-line starting of a standard motor, 5 to 7 as the typical range. For star-delta starting use about 2 to 3, and for a soft starter use the manufacturer's stated value, usually 2 to 4. If the nameplate shows a NEMA code letter, look up its locked-rotor kVA per HP for the exact figure.

faqs.q: Can I size the cable for the running current only?
faqs.a: No. Cables must carry the running current continuously, but breakers, contactors, and fuses must survive the inrush without tripping or welding. Size the cable for full-load current with the standard derating factors, then verify the protection co-ordinates with the starting current.

faqs.q: How do HP and kW relate?
faqs.a: 1 HP equals 746 W (0.746 kW) of mechanical output. This calculator converts automatically, so enter whichever unit is on the nameplate.

faqs.q: Why is power factor in the formula?
faqs.a: The supply must deliver both real power (which does the work) and reactive power (which magnetizes the motor). Power factor is the ratio of real to total power, so a lower power factor means more current for the same mechanical output.

faqs.q: Does this work for DC motors?
faqs.a: No. DC motor starting current depends on armature resistance and the starter used, which is a different calculation. This tool is for AC induction motors only.
